question.text: Will Judge McFadden have granted Comey's motion to dismiss the D.C. criminal information by November 13, 2026?
question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if, on or before November 13, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia issues an order in United States v. Comey, No. 1:26-cr-00229-TNM, granting James Comey's motion to dismiss the criminal information (ECF No. 11, including any amended or refiled version of that motion) and dismissing the criminal information in its entirety, with or without prejudice; an order granting the motion only in part, so that any count of the information survives, resolves No. It resolves No if the Court denies that motion or has issued no order granting it by that date. Resolution is based on the case docket in 1:26-cr-00229-TNM (case filings are compiled at https://www.nacdl.org/brief/United-States-v-Comey-(2)) or, if the docket is unavailable, on reporting by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).
question.fine_print: Dismissal of the criminal information on any other basis — for example, a motion by the government to dismiss, or the return of a grand jury indictment that supersedes the information — does not count as granting ECF No. 11, including where the Court denies that motion as moot. If the Court issues an order granting ECF No. 11 on or before November 13, 2026, but the order becomes public only after that date, the question still resolves Yes.

research:
I found no ruling on ECF No. 11 and no grand jury action as of November 2, 2026. Both remaining paths to a ruling point toward No unless McFadden grants the motion on the merits: an indictment would most likely make the motion moot, and a dismissal on another basis (for example the Speedy Trial Act) does not count.

## 1. Resolution source
- 2026-11-02 (when I checked): The NACDL tracker lists ECF 1 (Information, 10/05/26), ECF 6 (motion to dismiss and for emergency hearing, 10/09/26), ECF 11 (motion to dismiss, 10/16/26) and ECF 12 (government response, 10/23/26). It shows no order on any motion. It does not list ECF 14, the 10/26 unsealing order, so it runs behind the actual docket. [NACDL](https://www.nacdl.org/brief/United-States-v-Comey-(2))
- I could not reach CourtListener (HTTP 403), so I could not check the full live docket.

## 2. Current status
- As of 2026-11-02 I found no report of McFadden granting or denying ECF 11. Nothing has settled the question yet.
- 2026-10-30: McFadden took the motion under advisement. He asked "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?", said the case "turned on very novel issues," and noted DOJ could come back with an indictment within about two weeks. [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/)
- 2026-10-30: According to a search summary of The Hill (I could not open the page), he seemed to lean toward the defense reading that "indictment" in the 10-year provision means an actual grand jury indictment. He suggested waiting to see whether prosecutors get one, and noted the defense could renew its limitations arguments against any indictment. [The Hill](https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/6184780-comey-criminal-case-dismissal-hearing/)

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-11-02: In a separate D.C. case, Magistrate Judge Faruqui dismissed charges against former FBI officials Floris and Benavides, calling the probe "weaponization." This is context for the D.C. court's climate, not this case. [NY Post](https://nypost.com/2026/11/02/us-news/dc-federal-judge-tosses-case-against-fbi-officials-accused-of-lying-about-hunter-biden-laptop/)
- 2026-10-31: Commentary piece arguing the judge might throw out the case. [Townhall](https://townhall.com/news/mattvespa/2026/10/31/the-james-comey-national-security-leak-indictment-might-get-tossed-n2685635)
- 2026-10-30: The prosecutor told the court "We are still going to the grand jury very diligently" (Bloomberg, as quoted in search results) and said DOJ may bring more charges. [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-in-defense-secrets-case), [CNN](https://cnn.com/2026/10/30/politics/comey-motion-hearing-leak-charges)
- 2026-10-30: DOJ attorney Dustin Farahnak said evidence from April 2017 could give the government six more months to charge Comey. ABC described the following Thursday, November 5, as the last day to seek an indictment before the information is dismissed under the Speedy Trial Act. It was unclear whether McFadden would rule before then. He also said "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days" and warned against a "dawn raid." [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147)
- 2026-10-30: McFadden delayed his decision while DOJ pursues an indictment. [WTOP](https://wtop.com/us-politics/2026/10/lawyers-for-ex-fbi-director-james-comey-will-ask-a-judge-to-block-justice-department-prosecution/)

## 4. Base rates
- I found no clean base rate. Dismissing charges because a waiverless information did not satisfy a statute of limitations is a new question; the judge himself called the issues "very novel."
- How the fine print sorts the likely paths:
  - **Indictment by about November 5:** ECF 11 would likely be denied as moot or re-briefed against the indictment. Resolves No.
  - **No indictment:** the information could be dismissed under the Speedy Trial Act, which may not count as granting ECF 11. McFadden could also grant ECF 11 on the merits, which would count.
  - **Government moves to dismiss:** resolves No.
- Recent context: D.C. grand juries have more often declined to indict in politically charged cases (the judge's own remark). Comey's Eastern District of Virginia case was dismissed on appointment grounds within about two months of the indictment.

## 5. Other forecasts
Prices as of 2026-11-02 17:17 UTC:
- Kalshi, "Will James Comey's national defense information case be dismissed?" (this D.D.C. case): 22% for before Jan 1, 2027, and 89% for before Jul 1, 2027. This market counts dismissal on any basis, so it is broader than this question.
- Kalshi, Comey case dismissed (seems to be the Virginia case): 27% before Jan 1, 2027.
- Polymarket, "Comey charges dropped by Dec 31": 39%. It is ambiguous which case this covers.
- I found no market that asks specifically whether ECF 11 is granted by November 13.

## 6. Upcoming events before November 13
- About November 5: the reported Speedy Trial Act deadline for an indictment. A grand jury could indict, decline, or do nothing.
- A possible superseding indictment or new charges, which would likely moot ECF 11.
- A possible ruling from McFadden on ECF 11, or a dismissal on Speedy Trial grounds, if no indictment arrives.
- A possible government motion to dismiss or a new filing based on the April 2017 conduct.

I've finished searching and am writing up the findings. As of November 2, 2026, Judge McFadden has not ruled on ECF No. 11. At the October 30 hearing he signaled he would wait to see whether prosecutors get an indictment rather than rule right away. I found no reporting dated after October 30 about this case.

## 1. Resolution source

It shows no order on the motion. It doesn't list the unsealing order (ECF 14, 10/26), so it runs behind the real docket. [NACDL](https://www.nacdl.org/brief/United-States-v-Comey-(2))
- CourtListener blocked my fetch (403), so I couldn't check the full docket directly.

## 2. Current status

He said the case "turned on very novel issues" and asked, "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?" He also noted DOJ could come back two weeks later with an indictment. [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/)
- He also asked whether the issue would be moot if DOJ got an indictment, and said he could simply let the government try, since the dispute would go away if a grand jury refused. ## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-11-02: In a separate D.C. case, Magistrate Judge Faruqui dismissed a complaint against former FBI officials Floris and Benavides, calling the probe "weaponization." This is not the Comey case. [NY Post](https://nypost.com/2026/11/02/us-news/dc-federal-judge-tosses-case-against-fbi-officials-accused-of-lying-about-hunter-biden-laptop/)
- 2026-10-30: Prosecutor Dustin Farahnak said DOJ is "still going to the grand jury diligently." He cited new evidence of overt acts after October 5, 2016, hinting at activity into 2017 that could bring an indictment within the 10-year limit. [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/), [AJC](https://www.ajc.com/news/2026/10/judge-puts-off-decision-in-comey-case-as-prosecutors-pursue-new-indictment-against-ex-fbi-head/)

DOJ said the new evidence could extend its window by six months. McFadden quipped "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days" and warned against a "dawn raid." [ABC7](https://abc7news.com/story/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts-charge-3rd-time/20000350/)

CBS doesn't give the exact dates, so I couldn't independently confirm the November 5 deadline. [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/)

- A single Substack post claims a grand jury rejected one of three charges. It's unverified and should be treated with caution. [America Explained](https://amerex.substack.com/p/round-up-comey-indictment-emergency)

## 4. Base rates
- I found no clean base rate for rulings on challenges to a "waiverless information." The issue is novel; the judge himself called it "very novel."
- Related history: the Eastern District of Virginia Comey case was dismissed on November 24, 2025, about two months after indictment. D.C. grand juries have repeatedly refused indictments in politically sensitive cases (judge's remark, AJC).
- Judges typically rule on a contested, novel motion like this several weeks after argument. Only 14 days separate the hearing and the November 13 deadline, and the judge signaled he would wait.

## 5. Other forecasts (prices as of 2026-11-02 17:17 UTC)
- Kalshi, "Comey national defense information case (1:26-cr-00229, D.D.C.) dismissed": 22% before January 1, 2027; 89% before July 1, 2027. This is the closest match, but it is broader than this question: it likely counts dismissal on any basis and has a longer window.
- Kalshi, "Comey's criminal case dismissed" (unclear which case): 27% before January 1, 2027; 60% before July 1, 2027.
- Polymarket, "Comey charges dropped by Dec 31": 39%. This is ambiguous about which case it covers.
- I found no market specific to a grant of ECF 11 by November 13.

## 6. Upcoming events before resolution
- About 2026-11-05: the reported end of DOJ's 30-day pause and/or the claimed deadline to indict. Possible outcomes:
  - An indictment would likely make ECF 11 moot, which resolves No.
  - A grand jury refusal, or no indictment, could lead McFadden to rule on the motion.
  - DOJ's claimed six-month extension (likely based on the savings statutes) could become the next fight.
- The government could move to dismiss the information itself, which would not count as granting ECF 11.
- A possible arrest or new charges: the judge warned against a "dawn raid."
- 2026-11-11 (Veterans Day) is a federal holiday, which slightly shortens the court's working days.

forecasts.reasoning:
(a) About 11 days remain, until November 13, 2026. For Yes, Judge McFadden must issue an order granting ECF No. 11 (Comey's motion to dismiss) and dismissing the whole information, on the merits or at least explicitly granting that motion. Dismissal on Speedy Trial grounds, on a government motion, or because an indictment supersedes the information does not count, and neither does denying the motion as moot.

(b) Status quo: the motion is under advisement and the judge said he was inclined to wait. If nothing changes, no order issues and the question resolves No.

(c) Base rate: there is no clean reference class for this novel question. Federal judges seldom grant a defense motion to dismiss within two weeks of argument when they have openly said they prefer to wait. A rough prior for "a pending motion is granted within about two weeks, after the judge signaled delay" is about 10-15%.

(d) Evidence:
- For Yes:
  - On October 30, McFadden seemed skeptical of the government's reading that a waiverless information counts as an "indictment" for limitations purposes.
  - D.C. grand juries have recently declined politically charged cases. McFadden himself joked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days."
  - If no indictment comes by about November 5, the information is left exposed, and he might then rule on the merits.
  - The D.C. court climate looks hostile: Faruqui's November 2 dismissal in a related "weaponization" case.
- For No:
  - On October 30 he asked "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?" and chose to await grand jury action.
  - An indictment would most likely moot ECF 11.
  - If no indictment arrives, dismissal could come via the Speedy Trial Act or the government instead.
  - Kalshi prices dismissal of this case on any basis before January 1, 2027 at only 22%, and that is broader and longer than this question.

(e) Scenarios:
- No: a grand jury indicts around November 5, and McFadden denies ECF 11 as moot, inviting renewed limitations arguments against the indictment. Alternatively, there is no indictment, the government moves to dismiss or seeks a new filing based on the April 2017 conduct, and the judge dismisses on that basis.
- Yes: the grand jury declines or the government misses the November 5 window. The government still insists the information is valid and tolls limitations. McFadden then issues a written opinion around November 10 granting ECF 11 and holding that a waiverless information cannot satisfy the statute of limitations.

(f) Moving to a final number:
- I put an indictment by about November 5 at roughly 45%, which leads to No.
- Without an indictment, the chance of a ruling that specifically grants ECF 11 by November 13 is maybe 25-35%, because the other routes to dismissal compete with it.
- That gives about 0.55 × 0.3 ≈ 16%.
- Kalshi's 22% covers any dismissal by year end, which is a superset of this outcome, so this question should sit well below it.
- I adjust down slightly from 16% to about 11%.

Probability: 11%

(a) There are about 11 days left, to November 13, 2026. For Yes, Judge McFadden must issue an order granting ECF No. 11 and dismissing both counts of the information. Dismissal on any other basis does not count, including a government motion, a Speedy Trial Act dismissal, or a ruling that the motion is moot after an indictment.

(b) The status quo is No. On October 30 the judge took the motion under advisement and signaled he would wait for prosecutors' next move rather than rule now.

(c) Base rate: there is no clean reference class, since the judge himself called the issue "very novel." Federal judges rarely grant a pretrial merits dismissal within two weeks of argument when they have openly said they would wait for the government's next step. I put a rough prior at 10-15%.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:**
  - On October 30, reporting from The Hill, Politico and CBS described McFadden as skeptical of the government's maneuver and leaning toward reading "indictment" to mean an actual grand jury indictment.
  - He said "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days," and D.C. grand juries have recently declined to indict in politically charged cases.
  - If no indictment arrives by about November 5, he could dispose of the information by granting ECF 11.
- **For No:**
  - On October 30 he asked "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?" and indicated he would wait.
  - Prosecutors said they are "going to the grand jury very diligently." An indictment would most likely moot ECF 11.
  - A failed indictment could lead the government to dismiss the information itself, or to a Speedy Trial Act dismissal. Neither counts.
  - As of November 2, the docket shows no ruling.

(e) Scenarios:
- **No:** A grand jury returns an indictment around November 5. McFadden denies ECF 11 as moot and sets briefing on a renewed limitations motion against the indictment.
- **Yes:** The grand jury declines or the deadline passes without an indictment. The government refuses to dismiss, and around November 9 McFadden issues an opinion granting ECF 11 on limitations grounds, dismissing the information without prejudice.

(f) Adjustment: The Kalshi market at 22% for dismissal on any basis before January 1, 2027 is broader in both grounds and timing, so this question should sit well below it. I estimate:
- Chance of no indictment: about 45%.
- If no indictment, chance the judge specifically grants ECF 11, rather than the government dismissing or a Speedy Trial dismissal: about 30-35%.
- Chance the order comes by November 13: about 80%.

That gives roughly 11-12%. I add a small allowance for a merits ruling issued alongside an indictment, which is unlikely. I end slightly below my base rate.

Probability: 11%

(c) There is no clean reference class. Pending motions to dismiss in federal criminal cases rarely get granted within two weeks of argument, especially when the judge calls the issues "very novel" and has said he wants to wait. A base rate for a grant in this window is roughly 10%.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:**
  - On October 30, reporting described McFadden as skeptical of the government and as leaning toward the defense reading that "indictment" means a grand jury indictment.

(e) Scenarios:
- **No:** A grand jury returns an indictment by November 5. McFadden denies ECF 11 as moot and sets briefing on renewed limitations challenges against the indictment. Alternatively, the government voluntarily dismisses the information.
- **Yes:** The grand jury declines or DOJ misses November 5. McFadden then issues a short opinion granting ECF 11, holding that a waiverless information cannot satisfy the ten-year provision, and dismisses without prejudice.

(f) I start from a base of about 10%. I adjust up for the judge's apparent skepticism and the real chance of no indictment, which could prompt a merits grant soon after November 5. I adjust down because the resolution rules exclude many of the likely dismissal paths (moot, Speedy Trial, government dismissal), and because the broader any-basis market is only 22% even through year-end. I end at about 12%.

Probability: 12%

I move slightly up for his apparent skepticism of the government's position. Net, I land around 6%.
